extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, metaphysical writers, and literary critics (particularly English metaphysicians and readers of Coleridge)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging metaphysical/philosophical prose: choices about terminology, method (transcendental approach), style, audience expectations, and conceptual distinctions (e.g., imagination vs. fancy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technical terms in philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms are justified when they preclude confusion of thought and assist the memory by exclusive singleness of meaning; they help distinguish kinds (with abstraction of degrees) and avoid weary circumlocutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scholastic or technical phrases where they (1) preclude confusion, (2) assist memory by exclusive singleness of meaning, (3) correspond in interdependent or antithetical terms (sound correspondence), or (4) avoid tedious circumlocutions. Example usages cited: multeity instead of multitude; potence to express a specific degree of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neologisms permitted only by necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: New-coined or unusual words are an evil in themselves but may be justified if they serve conceptual clarity where no existing term is adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit neologisms sparingly when there is no positive existing term adequate to the purpose, and when the new term accords with the end (final cause) of terminology. Coleridge defends coinages like 'potenziate' when they express combinations or transfers of powers that existing vocabulary does not capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precision over picturability
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not restrict 'conceivable' to what can be represented by a distinct image; intellectual truths may be non-picturable and still valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the modern creed that only what can form a distinct image is a clear conception. The conceivable should not be reduced to the picturable; otherwise many valid intellectual notions are wrongly rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish limits of human faculties from limits of things
rubrics_metrics.description: The incapacity of the human mind to represent certain abstract notions concretely is a subjective limitation and should not be mistaken for an impossibility or negation in the object itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the common error of treating the mind's inability to form concrete images of abstract intellectual ideas as proof that those ideas are impossible in themselves. The passage: 'the mind cannot always adequately represent in the concrete... too often passes for an incongruity or impossibility in the object' is given as warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain systematic coherence; avoid aphoristic eclecticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical writing should preserve logical connexion and system; the practice of picking only plausible or showy aphorisms without logical structure (popular aphoristic eclecticism) is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'pick and choose whatever is most plausible and showy' while dismissing system and logical connection. Such eclecticism produces a 'popular philosophy' that undermines taste and faculty for genuine systematic thought; prefer organized, connected argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and address audience prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the varied expectations of readers (e.g., those who expect immediate utility, those morally or religiously alarmed by certain doctrines, or those wedded to familiar nomenclature) and respond appropriately in exposition and defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for an English readership (or readers oriented to practical utility), either show practical application or appeal to respected authorities (Coleridge cites Bacon). Be prepared to defend metaphysics against moral/religious prejudices and against objections rooted in alternative terminologies (Locke, Hume, Reid, Stewart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental method: seek the principle within knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcendental philosopher must seek 'the last in our knowing itself' (the ultimate principle of our knowledge) rather than inquire into an ultimate ground external to our knowing; self-consciousness is asserted as the fixed point and source/principle of possible knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, start from the act of self-consciousness as the primary principle of knowledge for the transcendental inquiry: 'The principle of our knowing is sought within the sphere of our knowing.' Be explicit about the grounding move and how self-consciousness functions as both subject and object in this account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate Imagination from Fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination and Fancy are distinct faculties: Imagination is the 'shaping and modifying' power (esemplastic), whereas Fancy is the 'aggregative and associative' power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing literature/philosophical prose, assign operations correctly: evoking and combining traces may belong to Fancy (aggregative/associative), while true Imagination performs unifying, shaping, or synthesizing operations. Coleridge disputes conflations (e.g., Wordsworth's) and insists on distinct definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the 'language of spirits' beyond surface diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic expression involves an interior, non-verbal 'sermo interior' that the language of words only vehicles; critics' failure to grasp meaning from surface phrasing may be due to lack of philosophical talent rather than to the work's vacuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing dense philosophical writing, consider whether difficulty arises from necessary depth or genuine obscurity. Do not automatically equate lack of surface clarity with lack of philosophical merit—examine whether an interior conceptual language is being manifested and whether the terminology is serving that deeper expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use terminology to expose and avoid vague nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: One aim of careful terminological choice is to expose and prevent the vagueness and insufficiency that enshroud errors in metaphysical schools; indefinite nomenclature often conceals error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ precise terms to reveal and counter errors that 'subsist... as they are concealed behind the mask of a plausible and indefinite nomenclature.' Be explicit about definitions and avoid tolerating vague or indefinite usage that permits hidden confusions.
